channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Climate and accident risk stacked up: a new study found human-caused warming roughly doubled the odds of Canada's summer wildfires, a chemical plant near São Paulo erupted in a fireball, and a record heatwave gripped Japan and Korea.
item.description:
Acute disruptions clustered again. A scientific attribution study concluded that human-caused climate change roughly doubled the likelihood of the tinder-dry conditions that fuelled Canada's massive summer wildfires; the Canadian Red Cross opened an appeal for British Columbia communities, and insurers braced for sizeable losses from fires around Spokane, Washington. In Brazil, a fire tore through a chemical plant in the São Paulo metropolitan area, sending up a dramatic fireball from an area holding around two million litres of flammable products — a direct industrial-safety event. Across Asia, a record heatwave pushed temperatures in greater Seoul toward 39°C, with thousands treated for heat illness since mid-May. Taken with Europe's drought (covered in a separate insight), the day underscored how weather and accident risk are converging on industry at once.

Industry Impact

Force-majeure events bear directly on the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry on both the risk and demand sides. The São Paulo plant fire is a pointed reminder that ACS and adjacent chemical operations handle large volumes of flammable material, keeping process safety, insurance cost and business-continuity planning front of mind. Wildfires, heat and drought disrupt logistics, raw-material availability and workforce productivity, and drive up insured losses that ultimately feed into operating costs. On the demand side, more frequent extreme weather strengthens the long-run case for weather-resistant, fire-retardant and infrastructure-repair coatings and sealants.

AP | Financial Post | AP | Le Figaro | AP

item.title: An explosive drone was found beside a Ukrainian aircraft at a German NATO logistics hub and briefly halted flights, while Ukraine became the world's top drone maker and a Russian drone-factory founder was car-bombed — the drone war nearing Europe.
item.description:
The conflict's frontier is widening. At Leipzig/Halle airport — a hub used by NATO and for Ukraine-bound logistics — security forces secured a drone rigged with an explosive and detonator near a parked Ukrainian Antonov transport plane, temporarily suspending operations; earlier a DHL cargo aircraft had struck an unidentified object while climbing away and made an emergency landing in Hanover. German authorities are investigating what looks like an attempted sabotage on European soil. The episode sits against a fast-militarising drone landscape: Ukraine has scaled up to become the world's leading manufacturer of unmanned systems, its strikes now reaching Russian energy and retail infrastructure, and the founder of Russian drone maker Uraldronzavod was critically injured by a car bomb near Yekaterinburg. Attacks on Black Sea ports and shipping are separately disrupting grain and oil flows.

Industry Impact

The direct read-through for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) is twofold. First, security: sabotage risk at European logistics and industrial nodes raises the premium on supply-chain resilience and site protection for chemical operators. Second, demand: the explosive growth of drone and unmanned-systems manufacturing — now a strategic industry in Ukraine and beyond — is a durable pull for high-performance structural adhesives, sealants, conformal and protective coatings and composites. ACS suppliers with defence and aerospace qualifications have a growing addressable market, alongside heavier compliance and dual-use export scrutiny.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | The Guardian | The Guardian | Business Recorder

item.title: Indonesia's economy grew 5.29% in the second quarter, its slowest in three quarters as consumer spending eased, even as Jakarta signed an investment pact with Saudi Arabia and ASEAN leaders pushed deeper regional integration.
item.description:
Southeast Asia's biggest economy lost a little steam. Indonesia's GDP grew 5.29% year-on-year in the second quarter, down from 5.61% in the first and the slowest in three quarters, as household and retail spending softened and layoff worries lingered; officials noted government spending rose sharply and stressed that growth still outpaced most global peers. Diplomatically and commercially, the region was busy: Indonesia and Saudi Arabia signed a memorandum to promote and protect direct cross-border investment, deepening Gulf–Southeast Asia capital ties, while at the ASEAN Conference 2026 Singaporean and Philippine ministers argued the bloc's strength lies in deeper integration and collective crisis response. Investors remained constructive on emerging-market debt, with the emerging-market local-currency bond market projected to extend 2025's 15% gain on high yields and solid growth.

Industry Impact

ASEAN is a priority growth region for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) demand, tied to construction, packaging, automotive and electronics manufacturing that is increasingly relocating into the bloc. A modest Indonesian slowdown tempers the near-term consumption story, but the deepening investment ties — especially Gulf capital flowing into Southeast Asian infrastructure and downstream industry — support the medium-term demand outlook. For ACS suppliers the signal is to treat ASEAN as a durable expansion theme while calibrating for softer near-term consumer demand in Indonesia specifically.

CNA | Antara News | Kompas.com | Antara News | CNA | Chinatimes.com

item.title: India's central bank kept its policy rate at 5.25% and raised its 2026/27 growth forecast to 6.7%, signalling confidence in the fastest-growing major economy, even as some economists expect momentum to ease later in the year before re-accelerating.
item.description:
India stayed on a steady, upbeat course. The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee held the repo rate — its main lending rate — at 5.25% and nudged its GDP growth forecast for the 2026/27 fiscal year up by 0.1 point to 6.7%, while trimming its inflation projection, a combination markets read as quietly positive. Analysts were more cautious on the trajectory: an ICICI Bank report projected growth would moderate in the second half of 2026/27 on a high base before accelerating to 7.2% in 2027/28. Beneath the macro numbers, India is pushing industrial ambitions: the government is streamlining approvals for "Semicon 2.0", the next phase of its roughly 760-billion-rupee semiconductor mission, and investor money is flowing into a growing space-technology start-up sector focused on propulsion, communications and in-orbit servicing.

Industry Impact

India remains one of the most attractive structural growth stories for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) demand, spanning construction, automotive, packaging and — increasingly — electronics as the semiconductor push builds out. A stable policy rate and a rising official growth forecast support continued capacity investment and consumer-durable demand, both positive for coatings and adhesives volumes. The semiconductor and space build-outs point to higher-value, technically demanding ACS applications over time. The main caveat is the flagged second-half slowdown, which argues for confident but staged expansion rather than assuming an uninterrupted climb.

The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times | LiveMint | The Economic Times

item.title: Chinese-made electric vehicles kept taking share in established markets — registrations in South Korea jumped 178.7% and three Chinese brands now rank in the global top ten — even as worldwide car sales fell about 5% in the first half.
item.description:
The pattern of Chinese automotive advance held. Registrations of China-made EVs in South Korea rose 178.7% year-on-year to nearly 70,000 units in the first half, credited to smart-vehicle features and competitive performance. Globally, three Chinese groups — BYD, Geely and others — now rank among the world's ten largest carmakers by first-half share, behind Toyota and Volkswagen. Overall the market was soft: the International Energy Agency said global car sales fell about 5% in the first half on policy shifts, fuel-price swings and economic strain, but EV sales rebounded strongly to a record in the second quarter. Europe offered a bright spot: UK new-car registrations rose 11.7% in July — the eighth straight month of growth and the best July since 2019 — powered by a 44.5% jump in EVs, while Turkey's electric-and-hybrid share passed 51%. German logistics firm Mosolf said it is profiting handsomely from shipping Chinese brands into Europe.

Industry Impact

Autos are a core demand pillar for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS), and the shift toward Chinese EVs reshapes where that demand sits and who controls the supplier relationships. EV platforms use different — and often more — bonding, sealing, thermal-management and coating chemistries than combustion cars, so the EV rebound is structurally positive for ACS volumes. But as Chinese OEMs take share in Korea, Europe and beyond, ACS suppliers face pressure to qualify into Chinese-brand supply chains and to follow their production footprints, while legacy Western OEM volumes — and the margins tied to them — erode.

China Daily | Cnyes.com | AP | MarketScreener | The Independent | Dünya | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Record-low water on Germany's Rhine, Neckar and Main is forcing chemical producers to weigh production cuts and ships to sail lighter, hydropower output has slumped, and the Danube fell low enough to expose sunken WWII warships.
item.description:
Europe's drought has moved from fields to factories. Germany's chemical industry warned that persistently low river levels are pushing it toward production cuts: when barges can carry less or stop entirely, costs rise and supply chains along the Rhine corridor seize up. Shipping on the Neckar and Main is already running lighter and slower. The energy system is feeling it too — utility EnBW said its run-of-river hydropower produced only 80% of the reference level in the first half, and just 63% in June. Downstream, the Danube dropped so low that WWII-era warships resurfaced near a Serbian port. Governments are scrambling on the agricultural front: France's agriculture minister unveiled a "no farmer left alone" support plan for heat, drought and fires and is canvassing EU peers about shipping in animal fodder. (See the force-majeure insight elsewhere in this alert for the wider wildfire and heat picture.)

Industry Impact

This is a direct, physical hit to the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) heartland. The Rhine is the logistics spine of Germany's chemical industry, and low water simultaneously raises inbound feedstock costs, constrains outbound shipments and — as producers now warn openly — threatens actual output. Reduced hydropower tightens the power market that energy-intensive chemical plants depend on. For ACS supply planning the implications are concrete: expect Rhine-corridor freight surcharges, potential allocation on some German-made intermediates, and a case for pre-positioning inventory or qualifying non-river logistics routes while the dry spell lasts.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | MarketScreener | Tagesschau | The Globe and Mail | Le Figaro | Réussir

item.title: German data turned cautiously less negative: car-industry sentiment jumped in July, machinery orders rose 5% in the first half, and a study found far fewer industrial jobs lost than assumed — though credit for smaller firms is tightening.
item.description:
After a grim run, a few green shoots appeared. The Ifo Institute's business-climate index for Germany's car sector rose six points in July on brighter expectations, though it stayed clearly negative at minus 15.6 — improvement, not recovery. The machinery and plant-engineering association VDMA said the price-adjusted value of orders rose 5% in the first half, with a striking 21% jump in June driven by large overseas contracts. A German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) study offered a longer-run reframing: the decline in industrial employment has been significantly smaller than commonly believed, with services-linked roles partly offsetting factory losses. The caveats are real, though. A KfW/Ifo study found small and medium-sized firms are finding it harder to get bank loans as lenders turn cautious in a weak economy, and employers' association BDA is fighting political resistance to pension reform it sees as vital to competitiveness.

Industry Impact

Germany is the heartland of Europe's Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) supply base, so any stabilisation in its industrial demand — especially autos and machinery — is welcome for resin, solvent and specialty-chemical suppliers. But the signals are tentative and uneven: sentiment is less bad rather than good, and tightening credit for the Mittelstand (the small and mid-sized firms that form the backbone of German manufacturing) could choke the very customers ACS producers serve. The read is a possible bottoming rather than an upturn — enough to justify watching order books closely, not enough to change capacity plans.

MarketScreener | WirtschaftsWoche | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Tagesschau | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Prime Minister Carney said Canada is ready to take a tougher stance if no deal is reached before the next round of US tariffs takes effect on 19 August, with autos, steel and aluminium at the centre of talks and a revived quota idea on the table.
item.description:
The clock is running on the North American trade file. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on 5 August that Ottawa is prepared to be "tougher" with Washington if the two sides cannot agree before US President Trump's next tariff round begins on 19 August, while stressing that the goal is still to cut the sector-specific tariffs — imposed under Section 232, a US law allowing tariffs on national-security grounds — that are battering Canada's steel, aluminium and auto industries. Negotiators led by Canada's chief trade envoy are in Washington reviving a proposal that would cap Canadian steel and aluminium exports under a quota system in exchange for lower US levies. Carney framed the talks as covering "all strategic sectors", autos included. Business sentiment at home is cautiously constructive: a KPMG survey found 51% of Canadian leaders expect federal economic measures to leave their firms better off over three years.

Industry Impact

North American supply chains for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) inputs are tightly integrated across the US–Canada border, so the outcome matters directly. A quota-for-relief deal on metals would ease costs for downstream manufacturing customers (autos, construction, packaging) that consume ACS products, whereas a breakdown before 19 August would raise input costs and disrupt cross-border flows of chemicals, paper and packaging. The episode reinforces a recurring theme in this alert: tariff regimes are fluid and deadline-driven, favouring contractual tariff-pass-through terms and flexible sourcing over fixed long-haul supply commitments.

The Globe and Mail | Financial Post | LiveMint | CBC | The Globe and Mail

item.title: A Federal Reserve governor said she is ready to raise interest rates if inflation does not ease, and Bank of Japan hike bets firmed after the US Treasury Secretary's comments — a hawkish tilt that helped push US equities to record highs.
item.description:
The rate-cut narrative is being turned on its head. Fed Governor Lisa Cook said inflation remains too high and that she would support raising the Fed's benchmark rate if price pressures persist — an unusually direct signal that the next move could be up, not down, for the world's anchor interest rate. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly likewise backed July's hold but warned inflation could prove a broader problem. Markets now put meaningful odds on a September hike. In Japan, expectations of a Bank of Japan rate rise in September firmed after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that Tokyo's currency intervention should be followed by rate increases to address fears the BOJ is "behind the curve". Paradoxically, US equities hit record highs for a fourth straight session as weak private-payroll data and falling bond yields kept investors hopeful — a market leaning one way while central bankers lean the other.

Industry Impact

Higher-for-longer, or even higher, rates in the US and Japan matter to Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) demand through the interest-rate-sensitive end markets — construction, housing and durable goods — that drive sealant, coating and adhesive volumes. A firmer dollar and yen dynamics also reshape input costs and export competitiveness. The key message for planning is that the widely assumed easing cycle may stall: financing costs for customers' projects could stay elevated into 2027, arguing for conservative volume assumptions in rate-sensitive segments and close attention to currency exposure.

MarketScreener | The Standard | Financial Post | Finance News Network | CNA | The Economic Times | MarketScreener

item.title: Trade-defence actions clustered around the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants chain: Pakistan set a 26.76% duty on Chinese adhesive tape, South Korea raided petrochemical makers over price-fixing, and Brazil moved to curb cheap Asian paper imports.
item.description:
Protectionism is reaching deep into the ACS value chain itself. Pakistan's National Tariff Commission imposed a definitive 26.76% anti-dumping duty on BOPP self-adhesive tape in jumbo rolls originating in China — a duty applied directly to an adhesives product, not just an upstream input. In South Korea, prosecutors raided seven petrochemical companies over alleged collusion on the prices of PVC and caustic soda, base chemicals used across coatings, plastics and construction materials — a sign of tougher antitrust enforcement in a sector already squeezed by overcapacity. Brazil, meanwhile, is preparing higher import duties to block dumped Asian paper and cardboard, with roughly 43% of its domestic capacity said to be idle. Company-level signals were mixed: Japan's Arakawa Chemical more than doubled first-quarter profit, and Taiwan will host a chemical-industry summit later in August focused on semiconductor materials and green chemistry.

Industry Impact

For Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants producers this is a double-edged environment. Anti-dumping duties like Pakistan's can protect local converters from underpriced imports — helpful where a producer manufactures in-market — but they also fragment global pricing and invite retaliation. The Korean price-fixing probe is a reminder that base-chemical inputs (PVC, caustic soda) sit under regulatory as well as cost pressure, which can feed through to input volatility. Net, ACS buyers should expect a more patchwork, duty-ridden trade map for both finished adhesives and feedstocks, rewarding regional manufacturing footprints and diversified supplier panels over single-source global sourcing.

Business Recorder | MarketScreener | Bumprom.ru | MarketScreener | Commercial Times | SCI

item.title: Washington will announce, as soon as 6 August, a 15% tariff plus minimum prices on polysilicon and solar products to shield US makers Wacker and Hemlock, while separately drafting a ban on Chinese-made optical components used inside data centres.
item.description:
Two material-level trade moves are landing at once. The Trump administration is preparing to impose a 15% tariff and price floors on polysilicon, silicon wafers, solar cells and modules — polysilicon being the refined, ultra-pure silicon at the heart of both solar panels and semiconductors. The stated aim is to protect US producers Wacker Chemie (a German chemical group with US plants) and Hemlock Semiconductor from cheaper Chinese supply, turning a key chemical feedstock into a strategic lever. In parallel, Washington is drafting rules to bar imports of new Chinese-made optical transceivers — the components that shuttle data between servers inside data centres — a move pushed by the FCC to strip Chinese content out of critical digital infrastructure; the news alone sent Chinese optical-component shares lower. Both fit a pattern of using tariffs and outright import bans to reshape technology supply chains around perceived security lines.

Industry Impact

The polysilicon action is the standout for chemicals: it shows Washington will apply tariffs plus price floors directly to a refined-chemical value chain, a template that could later reach other feedstocks and intermediates that Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers rely on. Price floors tend to lift the whole regional price level, not just imports, so US-based buyers of silicon-derived and solar-linked materials should expect higher costs. The data-centre component ban adds cost and complexity for the fast-growing electronics-and-cooling segment that consumes thermal, encapsulant and bonding chemistries — a demand driver worth watching, now wrapped in fresh sourcing risk.

BNN Bloomberg | The Standard | Financial Post | Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | The Economic Times

item.title: China hit back at a week of US measures — imposing case-by-case export controls on drones and parts bound for America and blacklisting several US entities — sharply raising tension weeks before a planned Xi–Trump summit, and it warned of more.
item.description:
Beijing moved from threats to action. China's Commerce Ministry announced a package of countermeasures on 5 August after Washington banned some foreign-made robots and power inverters (via the Federal Communications Commission) and blacklisted more than 40 Chinese firms over alleged forced labour. The measures put drones, their key components and related technologies on China's dual-use export-control list, meaning any shipment to the US now faces strict case-by-case review; Beijing also added US entities — among them Applied DNA Sciences, Stratum Reservoir and Altana Technologies — to its own countermeasure and "unreliable entity" lists. State media framed it as unavoidable self-defence, with the People's Daily urging a "cooperation list, not a control list". The clash lands as a string of smaller trade and technology disputes pile up ahead of Xi Jinping's planned September visit to Washington. Underlining China's leverage, its robot exports topped 12 million units in the first half and industrial-robot exports rose 18.6%.

Industry Impact

This is a direct supply-chain risk for anyone touching electronics, automation or drone-linked value chains — and a warning shot for chemicals. China's willingness to weaponise export controls on dual-use goods signals that specialty chemicals, rare earths and advanced materials could be next if tensions worsen. For Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) suppliers, the immediate exposure is via customers in electronics, robotics and defence, and the second-order risk is that China restricts feedstocks or intermediates. The pre-summit noise argues for mapping Chinese-origin dependencies now and lining up alternative sources before any escalation hardens.

Los Angeles Times | The Express Tribune | Lianhe Zaobao | China Daily | The Asahi Shimbun | South China Morning Post | Daily Times

item.title: A concrete plan to end the five-month US–Iran war emerged — an Oman-brokered deal giving Tehran a say over ships entering the Gulf — pushing oil lower as Washington quietly lifted some Iran-linked sanctions, though Hormuz traffic is still a trickle.
item.description:
For the first time the endgame looks real. According to regional and Iranian sources, Oman is brokering an arrangement to end the war in which Iran would gain a degree of control over vessels entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz — the sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. On the same hopes that a deal could reopen Hormuz, oil prices edged lower. Washington sent its own de-escalation signals, lifting US sanctions on several Iran-linked airlines and entities (including Iraq's Fly Baghdad and three aircraft), which officials stressed did not mark a policy shift. But the relief is fragile: ship-tracking data showed only about eight vessels passing through Hormuz on 4 August, far below the normal flow, and LNG shipping costs have jumped 73% month-on-month to their highest since 2022. US refiner Phillips 66 warned that war-driven supply disruptions could keep fuel margins elevated into 2027, with markets still short an estimated 7 million barrels a day.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, a credible path to ending the war is the first genuinely good news on input costs in months: a reopened Hormuz would relieve pressure on naphtha, solvents, resins and freight. But nothing has flowed yet — traffic is minimal, tanker and LNG costs are still extreme, and refiners are guiding to elevated margins into 2027. The prudent read is cautious optimism: keep hedges and buffer stocks in place, but begin scenario-planning for a cost normalisation if the Oman deal actually holds.

The Standard | Business Recorder | Chinatimes.com | The Express Tribune | China Economic Net | Anadolu Agency | Financial Post
